, الخرطوم , السودان 0 البرهان يعزي انجال السيد محمد عثمان الميرغني في رحيل والدهم - الجمعة 20 نوفمبر 2026 الخرطوم 21 نوفمبر 2026 – بث رئيس مجلس السيادة القائد العام للجيش السوداني تطمينات إلى أهالي مدينة الدمازين بإقليم النيل الأزرق، مؤكداً أن القوات المسلحة قادرة على التصدي لأي محاولات تستهدف المدينة. وتزامنت تصريحات البرهان التي أطلقها مساء الجمعة، مع سيطرة الدعم السريع على عدة بلدات في إقليم النيل الأزرق بعضها قريب من الدمازين، وهو ما دفع آلاف المواطنين إلى الفرار نحو وسط وشرق السودان. وقال البرهان في كلمة عقب تقديمه التعازي في وفاة زعيم الحزب الاتحادي الديمقراطي الأصل محمد عثمان الميرغني بالخرطوم بحري إن “المواطنين في الدمازين لا ينبغي أن يشعروا بالخوف، إن قوات الدعم السريع كانوا موجودين في ذات المنزل الذي أتحدث فيه” – في إشارة إلى أن تلك القوات كانت متواجدة في قلب العاصمة الخرطوم – مؤكداً على أن أي قوة تدخل مناطق جديدة ستجد نفسها في فخ لن تتمكن من الخروج منه. وشدد البرهان على أن القوات المسلحة وتلك المساندة لها ماضيتان في القتال حتى إنهاء التمرد واستعادة السيطرة على كامل الأراضي السودانية، قائلاً: “عهدنا معاكم وعهدنا مع الشهداء أن نمضي معكم لغاية ما نطهر البلد كلها شرقها وغربها، جنوبها وشمالها”. وأكد أن السودان لن يخضع لأي جهة تسعى إلى احتلال أراضيه أو فرض سيطرتها على مواطنيه، مشيراً إلى أن القوات تقاتل دفاعاً عن البلاد والمواطنين وحق السودانيين في الوجود والعيش بأمن وكرامة. وفي سياق متصل، أقر البرهان بوجود ضغوط معيشية وخدمية تواجه المواطنين، من بينها انقطاع الكهرباء والمياه ونقص بعض الاحتياجات الأساسية، لكنه أرجع جانباً كبيراً من هذه الأوضاع إلى ما وصفه بحرب اقتصادية تشنها الجهات التي تقف وراء الحرب، بهدف إضعاف الدولة والتأثير على معنويات الشعب السوداني. وقال إن موارد الدولة تذهب في الوقت الراهن إلى العمليات العسكرية، مؤكداً أن الأولوية تتمثل في إنهاء التمرد حتى لا تتكرر الأوضاع التي قادت إلى اندلاع الحرب في 15 أبريل 2023. وجدد البرهان تأكيده على أهمية وحدة السودانيين وتماسكهم، مستشهداً بالقيم الاجتماعية التي نشأ عليها المجتمع السوداني، ودور الطرق الصوفية، وعلى رأسها الطريقة الختمية، في ترسيخ معاني التسامح والتآخي والتراحم. وفي الشأن السياسي، دعا القوى والأحزاب السياسية إلى الاستعداد للانتخابات، مؤكداً أن الوصول إلى السلطة ينبغي أن يكون عبر صناديق الاقتراع، وليس من خلال الانقلابات العسكرية أو أي وسائل أخرى. الكلمات: أخبار السودان. إقليم بولاية جنوب دارفور غربي السودان لضربات بطائرات مسيّرة. وكثف الجيش خلال الأسابيع الأخيرة من الهجمات على نيالا، التي تُعد مركزاً حيوياً لقوات الدعم السريع ومقراً إدارياً لحكومة تأسيس الموازية للسلطات الرسمية، مستهدفاً تجمعات القوات، فيما تصيب بعض الضربات الأسواق. وقالت المنسقة المقيمة للأمم المتحدة ومنسقة الشؤون الإنسانية في السودان، دينيس براون، في بيان، إن “حي المَزاد بمدينة نيالا بالقرب من مقار منظمات إنسانية تعرض لهجمات متعددة أول من أمس الخميس”. وأشارت إلى أن العاملين في المجال الإنساني، من المنظمات الوطنية والدولية، يعملون على الأرض في جميع أنحاء البلاد بهدف إنقاذ الأرواح. وشددت على أن العاملين في المجال الإنساني وممتلكاتهم يتمتعون بالحماية بموجب القانون الدولي الإنساني. وأضافت: “إن ضربات الطائرات المسيّرة في البلاد، أينما وقعت، تتسبب في سقوط قتلى من المدنيين ومعاناة لا توصف”. ولم يتحدث البيان عن سقوط قتلى جراء الضربات، كما لم يُدن الهجمات التي لم ينسبها إلى أي طرف. والخميس، قالت الهيئة الوطنية للوصول الإنساني التابعة لحكومة تأسيس الموازية إن الجيش قصف محيط مقار المنظمات الإنسانية في نيالا، مما أدى إلى مقتل 27 مدنياً، معظمهم من العاملين في المنطقة والباعة المتجولين. وأشارت إلى أن طائرة مسيّرة قصفت موقعاً جنوب مبنى الوكالة السودانية للإغاثة والعمليات الإنسانية التابعة للدعم السريع، حيث تضم المنطقة مقار منظمات أطباء بلا حدود وكير الدولية وجمكو وMC، إضافة إلى منظمة نيدو. وطالبت الهيئة بضرورة إجراء تحقيق مستقل في مصدر الضربة والهدف الذي وُجّهت إليه. وأوضحت أن المنظمات العالمية أخطرت سابقاً طرفي النزاع بموقع المنطقة وطبيعة استخدامها للعمل الإنساني والدبلوماسي. الكلمات: أخبار السودان. أطباء بلا حدود الأمم المتحدة الجيش السوداني السودان الطائرات المسيرة القانون الدولي طاولة الحوار ووقف العمليات العسكرية، مع التركيز على ضمان احترام سيادة السودان ورفض التدخلات الخارجية. وتكتسب الاجتماعات الوزارية ومذكرات التعاون أهمية في دعم المؤسسات السودانية وسط الأزمة الإنسانية sudan.content: السودان يستعد لاستئناف إنتاج اللقاحات البيطرية - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English السبت , 21 نوفمبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية اختيار المحرر السودان يستعد لاستئناف إنتاج اللقاحات البيطرية اختيار المحرر السودان يستعد لاستئناف إنتاج اللقاحات البيطرية 21 نوفمبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , السودان 0 وصول شحنة من بذور اللقاحات البيطرية الى السودان - السبت 21 نوفمبر 2026 الخرطوم 21 نوفمبر 2026 – كشفت السلطات السودانية عن وصول شحنة من بذور اللقاحات البيطرية من المعمل المرجعي للاتحاد الإفريقي بأديس أبابا، تمهيداً لاستعادة إنتاج اللقاحات في السودان. وتواجه الثروة الحيوانية في السودان تداعيات النزاع المسلح، والتي شملت تدمير البنية التحتية، وشح المراعي، ونقص الأعلاف وارتفاع أسعارها، إلى جانب تراجع الخدمات البيطرية وتضرر المزارع وتعرضها للنهب. وأدى ذلك إلى فقدان ولاية الخرطوم ما بين 69% و80% من قطيعها، بما يعادل نحو 320 ألف رأس من الأبقار، فيما فقدت ولاية الجزيرة نحو 100 ألف رأس من الأبقار. كما تضررت المحاجر والمسالخ والمصانع، وانقطعت سلاسل التوريد وطرق نقل المواشي، ما أثر على حركة الرعي والتصدير. وأعلنت وزارة الثروة الحيوانية والسمكية، في بيان صحفي السبت، وصول شحنة من بذور اللقاحات البيطرية من المعمل المرجعي للاتحاد الإفريقي بأديس أبابا، تمهيداً لاستعادة إنتاج اللقاحات بالمعمل المركزي وتعزيز قدراته في مكافحة الأمراض وحماية الثروة الحيوانية. وأوضحت مديرة المعمل المركزي للبحوث البيطرية، خالدة عبد العزيز خليفة، أن الشحنة تضم بذور لقاحات طاعون المجترات الصغيرة، والجلد العقدي، والالتهاب البلوري للأبقار والماعز، والحمى الفحمية، والساق الأسود، مشيرة إلى أن توفير هذه البذور يمثل بداية لاستعادة إنتاج اللقاحات البيطرية في السودان. وأضافت أن وصول الشحنة يشكل خطوة متقدمة في مسيرة إعادة تأهيل المعمل واستعادة قدراته الإنتاجية، ويمهد لعودته إلى توفير اللقاحات اللازمة لمكافحة الأمراض التي تهدد الثروة الحيوانية، بما يسهم في تطوير الخدمات البيطرية وتعزيز الأمن الصحي للقطيع القومي، وتقليل الاعتماد على استيراد اللقاحات من الخارج. وأعربت مديرة المعمل عن تقديرها لوزارة الثروة الحيوانية ووزارة المالية، والمعمل المرجعي للاتحاد الإفريقي، وأبناء المعمل في المهجر، مثمنة دعمهم ومساندتهم للمؤسسة، ودورهم في تذليل الصعوبات والمساهمة في توفير بذور اللقاحات، بما يعزز فرص استئناف الإنتاج ومواصلة المعمل دوره في خدمة قطاع الثروة الحيوانية بالسودان. وأدت الحرب المستمرة في السودان منذ أبريل 2023 إلى تضرر البنية التحتية البيطرية وتوقف إنتاج وتوزيع اللقاحات، ما انعكس سلباً على صحة الماشية والأمن الغذائي. كما تسببت الأعمال العسكرية وتدمير منشآت ومقار البحوث البيطرية في الخرطوم في تعطيل إنتاج اللقاحات والأمصال، فيما أسهمت انقطاعات الكهرباء وتعطل سلاسل التبريد والإمداد في صعوبة حفظ اللقاحات وتوزيعها على الولايات. وانعكس تراجع التحصين الدوري ونقص الأدوية العلاجية في عودة أمراض كانت تحت السيطرة، بينها التسمم الدموي، والحمى الفحمية، وجدري الأغنام والماعز، والحمى القلاعية، مع تسجيل حالات نفوق في مناطق الإنتاج. وفي سياق معالجة أزمة الأعلاف ومهددات القطاع، أصدر رئيس الوزراء، كامل إدريس، الأسبوع الماضي، قراراً بإعفاء الذرة الشامية المستوردة من الرسوم الجمركية، بما يشمل رسم الوارد والرسم الإضافي، إلى جانب إعفاء أمباز فول الصويا من رسم الوارد، في خطوة تستهدف سد الفجوة العلفية والحد من ارتفاع تكاليف الإنتاج وأسعار المنتجات الحيوانية. وتُقدّر الفجوة العلفية في السودان، حتى قبل الحرب والجفاف، بنحو 14 مليون طن من المادة الجافة، فيما يمثل استمرار تصدير الأعلاف والمواد الداخلة في صناعتها، رغم العجز المحلي، تحدياً أمام استدامة قطاع الثروة الحيوانية. الكلمات: أخبار السودان. اقتصاد السودان الأعلاف الأمن الغذائي التنمية الاجتماعية بولاية الخرطوم، صديق فريني، عن بلوغ أعداد الأشخاص ذوي الإعاقة في الولاية نحو 20 ألف شخص، أي ما يعادل 2.5% من سكان العاصمة السودانية. وأكد فريني أن الحرب فاقمت معاناتهم وأدت إلى تسجيل إعاقات حركية وسمعية وبصرية جديدة، بينها حالات بتر أطراف لأطفال، جراء القصف المدفعي العشوائي، وهو ما دفع الوزارة للبدء في حصر ميداني شامل عبر سجلات المساعدات في المحليات لرصد الزيادة الناتجة عن الحرب. أخبار مقترحة من قطر ومصر إلى قمة البحرين والسعودية.. المواجهات العربية في تاريخ مونديال الناشئين مشاورات بين مصر والسودان وإريتريا والكونغو حول الأمن المائي والإقليمي وفي مقابلة مع منصة " الجزيرة- السودان "، أعدها الصحفي محمد الزين، أوضح الوزير فريني أن المرحلة المقبلة تتطلب الانتقال من مفهوم "الرعاية التقليدية والاستجابة الطارئة" إلى "التمكين الاقتصادي والإنتاج" وإشراك ذوي الإعاقة في جهود إعادة الإعمار. وفي هذا السياق، تتجه حكومة الولاية لتخصيص أكثر من 15% من فرص التمويل المتاحة لدعم مشروعاتهم الاقتصادية بوصفه بديلا عمليا يعزز استقلاليتهم في ظل محدودية التوظيف، بالتزامن مع توجيه والي الخرطوم بتفعيل قانون الأشخاص ذوي الإعاقة، وهو ما يرى الوزير أنه كفيل بمعالجة نحو 70% من المعوقات التي تواجههم. وعلى صعيد الخدمات والبنية التحتية، أشار الوزير إلى أن الحرب تسببت في تدمير وسرقة معدات عدد من المدارس والمراكز التأهيلية المتخصصة مثل "مركز السلامة" للإعاقة السمعية، بينما تواصل مراكز أخرى نشاطها مثل "مركز النور للمكفوفين". ورغم إعادة تشغيل معظم المؤسسات الصحية، لا تزال صعوبة التنقل وضعف منظومة التأمين الصحي يشكلان عائقا كبيرا، وفق الوزير السوداني، لذا تبحث الولاية دمج هيئة التأمين الصحي بالخرطوم في الصندوق القومي أو إقامة شراكة أوسع بينهما لتوسيع التغطية العلاجية. وبحسب الوزير السوداني، لم تقتصر تداعيات الحرب على الإصابات الجسدية وفقدان مصادر الرزق والنزوح إلى بيئات غير مهيأة، بل امتدت لتشمل اضطرابات نفسية حادة جراء الخوف والتوتر المستمر. ومع ذلك، أشاد فريني بمستويات التكافل المجتمعي في استضافة النازحين، منوها بالدور الإيجابي للأشخاص ذوي الإعاقة أنفسهم خلال الأزمة، حيث نظموا مبادرات للتبرع بالدم أثبتت رغبتهم في المشاركة المجتمعية الفاعلة لا مجرد تلقي المساعدات. sudan.content: الانتقال إلى المحتوى الرئيسي Reporting the Changing World وكالتنا لمحة عن تاريخ الوكالة التوصيف الوظيفي نظام إدارة الجودة مبادئ-النشر السياسات-الخاصة-بالإعلام-الاجتماعي سياسة الخصوصية والكوكيز سياسة الإفصاح RSS السودان يعلن خطة لإنشاء موانئ متخصصة على البحر الأحمر التواصل بيانات الاتصال طلبات الاشتراك Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 تركيا الدول العربية دولي اقتصاد رياضة تقارير EDITION Türkçe English BHSC Pусский Français العربية Kurdî کوردی Shqip فارسی македонски Bahasa Indonesia Español كوب 31 أنطاليا 3 سنوات من الإبادة الاعتداءات في الضفة الغربية السودان السودان يعلن خطة لإنشاء موانئ متخصصة على البحر الأحمر بينها ميناء في سواكن لاستيراد الغاز الطبيعي وتخزينه عقب توقيع اتفاق مع شركة تركية لإنشائه، وفق وزير البنية التحتية والنقل سيف النصر التجاني هارون.. Adel Abdelrheem 21 نوفمبر 2026 • تحديث : 21 نوفمبر 2026 SUDAN عادل عبد الرحيم/ الأناضول أعلنت الحكومة السودانية، خطة لإنشاء موانئ متخصصة على امتداد ساحل البلاد على البحر الأحمر، البالغ طوله نحو ألف كيلومتر، بينها ميناء في مدينة سواكن شمالي شرق البلاد لاستيراد الغاز الطبيعي وتخزينه، مشيرا إلى توقيع اتفاق مع شركة تركية لإنشائه. وقال وزير البنية التحتية والنقل، سيف النصر التجاني هارون، حسب ما نقلت عنه وكالة الأنباء السودانية "سونا" مساء الجمعة، إن ميناء بورتسودان من أقدم الموانئ السودانية، وإن تحديثه وميكنته باتا ضرورة في ظل نمو التجارة واتجاه العالم نحو تحديث الموانئ، رغم المخاوف من الاستغناء عن العنصر البشري. وأوضح أن الخطة تشمل إنشاء موانئ في أوسيف وأبو عمامة ومحمد قول ومواقع أخرى، بينها موانئ مخصصة للثروة الحيوانية والمعادن ومدخلاتها، وميناء للركاب، لا سيما في موسم الحج، وميناء للبضائع والحاويات، وآخر لخدمة الدول المجاورة. وأشار هارون، إلى توقيع اتفاق قبل أقل من شهر مع شركة تركية لإنشاء ميناء في سواكن لاستيراد الغاز الطبيعي وتخزينه، دون ذكر تفاصيل إضافية عن التكلفة أو الشركة المنفذة لكنه أوضح أن المشروع يهدف إلى توفير الغاز بأسعار أقل وتيسير الحصول عليه، وقد يلبي احتياجات الدول المجاورة. وأضاف أن الوزارة تخطط لإنشاء حوض لبناء السفن في بورتسودان أو سواكن، بالاستفادة من الخبرة التركية في بحر إيجة والبحر الأسود، موضحا وأن الحوض سيكون الوحيد من نوعه على ضفتي البحر الأحمر. ولفت هارون، إلى وجود طلبات ووعود من تركيا وقطر والسعودية وروسيا لتحديث ميناء بورتسودان شمالي شرق البلاد وإنشاء ميناء أو ميناءين على البحر الأحمر. وأضاف أن مشروع إيصال مياه الشرب من نهر عطبرة إلى ساحل البحر الأحمر سيتيح استغلال الساحل السوداني بالكامل. ويهدف المشروع إلى إنهاء أزمة العطش المزمنة في ولاية البحر الأحمر وتوفير إمداد مائي مستدام يدعم التوسع السكاني والاستثماري على طول الشريط الساحل". ويُعد ميناء بورتسودان الميناء الرئيسي في السودان، ويضم الميناء الجنوبي المخصص للحاويات، والميناء الشمالي الذي يُستخدم منفذا رئيسيا لاستيراد السلع الاستراتيجية، مثل الوقود والقمح والسكر. وتشمل الموانئ السودانية أيضا ميناء بشائر المخصص لتصدير نفط دولة جنوب السودان، وميناء عثمان دقنة في سواكن، المخصص لنقل sudan.content: مرصد حقوقي يتهم «الدعم السريع» بقتل مدنيين في غرب كردفان - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English السبت , 21 نوفمبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية اختيار المحرر مرصد حقوقي يتهم «الدعم السريع» بقتل مدنيين في غرب كردفان اختيار المحرر مرصد حقوقي يتهم «الدعم السريع» بقتل مدنيين في غرب كردفان 21 نوفمبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , كردفان 0 منازل مدنيين تحترق في بلدة أبو قلب بغرب كردفان عقب غارة جوية لطيران الجيش- الأحد 15 نوفمبر 2026 الأبيض 20 نوفمبر 2026 – اتهم مرصد حقوقي، السبت، قوات الدعم السريع بقتل ثلاثة مواطنين في منطقة “أبو قلب” بولاية غرب كردفان، فيما تحدث ناشطون عن عمليات قتل ذات طابع عرقي ترتكبها القوات ذاتها ضد المدنيين في البلدة. وخلال الأسبوع المنصرم، شن الطيران الحربي التابع للجيش السوداني غارات جوية مكثفة مستهدفاً أعداداً كبيرة من القرى في محيط مدن النهود وغبيش وأبو زبد وود بندة بولاية غرب كردفان، وهي مناطق خاضعة لسيطرة الدعم السريع، ويأتي هذا التصعيد الجوي بالتزامن مع تقدم متسارع يحرزه الجيش تجاه معاقل الدعم السريع في غرب كردفان. وأدى التصعيد الجوي والتقدم المتسارع للجيش إلى إجبار أعداد كبيرة من المدنيين على الفرار نحو إقليم دارفور، بينما فضّل آخرون النزوح نحو مدينة الأبيض بولاية شمال كردفان، بعد نهب الأسواق والمنازل من قبل عناصر الدعم السريع. وقال مرصد كردفان في بيان إن “المواطن صلاح بخيت قُتل إثر إطلاق مسلحين من الدعم السريع النار عليه مباشرة، في منطقة أبو قلب بعد اتهامه بتأييد الجيش، وذلك وفقاً لمعلومات تلقاها المرصد من ناجين”. وأضاف أن مسلحين آخرين قتلوا مواطنين اثنين، هما أبو هشيم محمد وعمر محمد علي، في قرية الشنابلة “الدميرة” المجاورة لمنطقة أبو قلب، قبل أن ينهبوا أبقارهم. وأشار البيان إلى أن الحادثتين وقعتا بالتزامن مع تفاقم الأوضاع الأمنية والإنسانية في المنطقة، التي تعرضت خلال الأسبوع الماضي لقصف جوي مكثف بواسطة طيران الجيش السوداني، أسفر عن مقتل 17 مواطناً على الأقل ونزوح نحو ثلاثة آلاف شخص. واعتبر المرصد استهداف المدنيين وقتلهم ونهب ممتلكاتهم انتهاكاً خطيراً لقواعد القانون الدولي الإنساني، التي تلزم أطراف النزاع بتوفير الحماية للمدنيين وعدم استهدافهم، مشيراً إلى أن هذه الانتهاكات قد ترقى إلى جرائم حرب تستوجب التحقيق والمساءلة. ودعا المنظمات الحقوقية والإنسانية والجهات المعنية إلى رصد الانتهاكات وتوثيقها بصورة مستقلة وحفظ الأدلة تمهيداً لمحاسبة المسؤولين عنها أمام آليات العدالة المحلية والدولية. وطالب بتوفير الحماية العاجلة للمدنيين والنازحين في منطقة أبو قلب، وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية والطبية إلى المصابين والمتضررين. وأبو قلب هي رئاسة وحدة إدارية تتبع لمحلية أبو زبد، وتقع على بعد نحو 17 كيلومتراً شمال شرقي المدينة، وتضم 49 قرية يقدر عدد سكانها الإجمالي بنحو 10 آلاف نسمة. من جانبها، اتهمت غرفة طوارئ دار حمر قوات الدعم السريع بارتكاب مجازر وانتهاكات وصفتها بالوحشية بحق المدنيين في أبو قلب، وقالت إن قائد القوات بالمنطقة حسين برشم حرّض علناً على استهداف السكان على أساس عرقي. وذكرت الغرفة، في نداء استغاثة، أن الانتهاكات شملت عمليات قتل وذبح ونهب وتهجير قسري، مشيرة إلى وقوع عمليات قتل في سوق أبو قلب، إلى جانب تصفية ثلاثة مواطنين رمياً بالرصاص في قرية الدميرة. وأضافت أن الدعم السريع اجتاحت ونهبت قرى “بوزة، جر العسل، حلة أبكر، أولاد مهاجر، سوق الظل، القريش” فضلاً عن عشرات القرى المجاورة. وحذرت الغرفة من موجات نزوح قسري واسعة وتقطع السبل بمئات الأسر في مناطق “قوز حرينديب، أبوجلق، الحمير، الرقيبة، أمدفيس”، مطالبة الجهات المختصة والأجهزة النظامية والمنظمات الحقوقية والإنسانية بالتدخل العاجل لإنقاذ المدنيين والأسر العالقة. الكلمات: أبو زبد أبو قلب أخبار السودان. الأبيض الجيش السوداني السودان النزوح في السودان حقوق الإنسان دار حمر غرب كردفان قوات الدعم السريع مرصد كردفان مقالات ذات صلة منع نقل السلع من «الشمالية» إلى مناطق سيطرة الدعم السريع تحالف ثوري يرفض تولي شركة أجنبية للاصلاح الإداري حريقان يقضيان على 30 منزلاً في قريتين بشمال دارفور مشاورات بين الحريةو ethiopia.content: Ethiopia faces risk of regional war ahead of COP32 climate summit Updates Red Mail 22° Tel Aviv-Jaffa Search Main Israel News Mideast & World News Tech & Digital Real Estate Finance Lifestyle Health & Science Jewish World Travel More Channels Opinions Magazine Sports Food Weather Podcasts Sites & Sources Ynet Calcalist yad2 ynetespanol Вести mynet Contact Contact us Privacy Policy Terms of Use Accessibility Statement Opinion Ethiopia faces risk of regional war ahead of COP32 climate summit Opinion: As Ethiopia prepares to host the COP32 climate summit in 2027, escalating tensions with Eritrea, Sudan and other regional rivals threaten stability in the Horn of Africa, raising concerns over Red Sea security and Israel's strategic interests Amine Ayoub | Add a comment Print Find an error? Report us Related Topics Ethiopia Climate change Addis Ababa From November 8 to 19, 2027, thousands of world leaders, climate negotiators, scientists and financiers will gather in Addis Ababa for 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32). Ethiopia has secured the presidency of the United Nations climate summit, a major diplomatic achievement that places the seat of the African Union at the center of global climate finance and renewable energy talks. Ethiopian officials have presented the event as proof of the country’s emergence as a green powerhouse, citing the Green Legacy reforestation campaign and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Africa’s largest hydroelectric facility. Gallery The security picture has deteriorated quickly. Forces loyal to Ethiopia’s federal government in Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, after recapturing the city from Tigrayan rebels on Oct. 4 ( Photo: Obtained by REUTERS ) Yet the same government is preparing for that spotlight while its neighborhood slides toward confrontation. Ethiopia’s greatest diplomatic success may become a practical constraint on its regional ambitions. Hosting COP32 creates reputational, financial and diplomatic incentives for restraint that Addis Ababa cannot easily ignore. Whether those incentives prove strong enough remains an open question with direct implications for Israel’s security along the Red Sea. The security picture has deteriorated quickly. Tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea escalated after fighting resumed between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan units in September 2026 and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations in response to Addis Ababa's decision to close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats. Troop concentrations near Badme, the flashpoint of the 1998–2000 war, have raised fears of direct confrontation. ACLED reported artillery exchanges and clashes near Badme on November 12 and 13, although Reuters could not independently verify direct fighting between the two armies. The African Union has called for restraint as the risk of wider fighting grows. Ethiopia’s long-standing search for sovereign Red Sea access compounds the problem. The 2024 memorandum with Somaliland triggered sharp opposition from Somalia, which views any arrangement that challenges its territorial integrity as unacceptable. Subsequent diplomacy produced the Ankara Declaration of December 11, 2024. Under that Turkish-facilitated agreement, Ethiopia and Somalia committed to negotiate reliable Ethiopian sea access under Somali sovereignty. The original memorandum created a crisis. The later framework established a different, still fragile path. Progress remains limited and distrust persists on both sides. These disputes have drawn in other regional actors. The October 4 El Alamein Declaration brought Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia together around sovereignty, territorial integrity and regional stability. The text affirms that Red Sea governance belongs to littoral states and rejects unilateral Nile measures that harm downstream countries. It also calls for peaceful solutions and does not name Ethiopia as an adversary. Even so, the declaration functions as a strategic counterweight to Ethiopian influence in both the Nile Basin and the Red Sea corridor. Cairo’s decision to deepen this coordination under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi prioritizes pressure over mediation. Cairo's close coordination with Khartoum, Asmara and Mogadishu increases diplomatic pressure on Addis Ababa. Although the declaration invokes peaceful solutions, its coordination framework strengthens a regional alignment whose positions on Nile waters, Somaliland and Red Sea governance frequently clash with Ethiopian interests. Red Sea ( Photo: Konoplytska/Shutterstock ) The Sisi regime has long treated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as a national security issue. Its regional posture amplifies zero-sum competition rather than reducing it. Sudan adds another layer of friction. Khartoum accuses Addis Ababa of supporting the Rapid Support Forces. Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing Tigrayan rebels. Both sides deny the charges. With Sudan already engulfed in civil war, any spillover across the shared border would further destabilize the region and multiply the risks facing civilian populations already suffering from displacement and food shortages. A separate diplomatic rupture between Somalia and the United Arab Emirates has complicated the picture further. Mogadishu expelled the UAE ambassador and earlier canceled agreements on ports, defense and security cooperation. Abu Dhabi rejected the accusations as escalatory. Because Gulf states maintain deep stakes in Red Sea ports and security arrangements, the dispute feeds uncertainty that reaches Addis Ababa’s own calculations. The Somalia-UAE confrontation remains secondary to the core state rivalries, yet it illustrates how quickly bilateral disputes can unsettle an already tense environment. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of these risks. It links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and carries a significant share of global maritime traffic. Any expansion of interstate conflict or further fragmentation of Somalia’s security landscape would create openings for armed groups. Al-Shabaab and residual ISIS-linked networks already operate in the region. They do not require control of capitals to threaten shipping lanes or project violence. Iran-backed Houthi forces have separately demonstrated the ability to disrupt traffic through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb. These threats exist independently. Together they make instability in the Horn a direct concern for Israel. The Red Sea is a strategic corridor for Israel , connecting the region to Asian and East African trade while exposing its southern maritime approaches to hostile forces. Bank of Israel research found that maritime imports from Asia and Oceania amounted to approximately $20 billion in 2023, around one-fifth of Israel's civilian imports. Although shipping diversions following Houthi attacks did not significantly reduce Israeli imports, they demonstrated how instability around Bab el-Mandeb can force vessels onto substantially longer routes and complicate maritime security. A wider crisis in the Horn would expand the operational space available to radical networks whose activities already endanger open sea lanes. Egypt’s contribution under Sisi has been to reinforce competitive alignments rather than to lower temperatures. A foreign policy that prioritizes short-term pressure on Ethiopia is not a stabilizing force. It is a risk multiplier for every state that relies on a secure Red Sea, including Israel. This is the context in which COP32 becomes more than a climate conference. Hosting the summit places Ethiopia under sustained international scrutiny. Foreign ministries, development banks, corporate sponsors and security services will examine the host country’s stability, airspace safety and regional relationships. This scrutiny is already underway. A joint UNFCCC and UN security mission visited Addis Ababa in July 2026 to assess venue, accommodation, transport, security and health preparations. Discussions on the host-country agreement have also begun. Ethiopia cannot afford a full-scale regional war in the months leading to November 2027 without damaging the credibility, attendance and financial success of the event. Major delegations and private investors can revise their plans if northern Ethiopia descends into cross-border fighting or if regional tensions dominate the agenda. Climate vulnerability and political conflict reinforce each other across the Horn. Drought, erratic rainfall, food insecurity and displacement place additional strain on governments already managing internal wars and mutual suspicion. If Addis Ababa intends to present itself as a leader in climate adaptation and cross-border resilience, partners will expect evidence of cooperation closer to home. Ethiopia has already begun framing COP32 as an inclusive platform for dialogue and climate finance delivery. That positioning creates leverage. The summit cannot resolve territorial disputes or replace direct negotiations. It can, however, raise the cost of escalation. Reputational damage, delayed climate financing, postponed investment and diminished international standing are concrete risks. Those risks give Ethiopian decision-makers incentives for restraint that did not exist before the country won the right to host. The prestige of the summit and the economic stakes attached to it may yet encourage cooler calculations in Addis Ababa and among its neighbors in the months ahead. COP32 will not settle the Nile dispute, resolve Ethiopia's maritime ambitions or erase the grievances separating Addis Ababa from its neighbors. But it can make escalation more costly for a government seeking to present itself as a global climate leader. Ethiopia's real test is whether it can translate international prestige into restraint at home and diplomacy abroad. For Israel, the question is whether the states surrounding the Red Sea can contain their rivalries before armed groups and external powers exploit the resulting instability. Amine Ayoub, a fellow at the Middle East Forum, is a policy analyst and writer based in Morocco. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is facing escalating tensions with regional rivals Eritrea and Sudan, raising concerns about potential conflict ahead of the COP32 climate summit scheduled for November 2027 in Addis Ababa. As Ethiopia prepares to host this significant event, which aims to position the country as a leader in climate finance and renewable energy, the deteriorating security situation poses a challenge to its diplomatic ambitions. Recent clashes near the contested Badme region and strained relations with Eritrea have heightened fears of direct confrontation. Additionally, Ethiopia's quest for access to the Red Sea has sparked opposition from Somalia, complicating regional dynamics. The African Union has called for restraint, but the involvement of other nations, including Egypt and Sudan, adds pressure on Ethiopia. The COP32 summit could serve as a platform for dialogue, but it also places Ethiopia under international scrutiny, making it imperative for the government to manage regional tensions to ensure the event's success and maintain its credibility.

Opinion November 21, 2026 Updated: November 21, 2026 Why Ethiopia Has Not Found Peace — and How Ethiopians Can Build It November 21, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber An evidence-based analysis of conflict, governance, and pathways to a durable settlement Publication draft prepared for review and attribution by the intended publisher. This is an independent analytical draft, not an endorsement by any organization. The author (file photo) Aklog Birara (Dr) Executive summary Ethiopia’s experience since 2018 is not a simple story of a peace prize followed by war. It is a story of an initially promising opening that did not resolve deeper struggles over political legitimacy, The newly appointed Prime Minister of Ethiopia Abiy Ahmed Ali managed to do two things simultaneously: charmed Ethiopians and the international community presenting himself and his party as reformists; and b) dismantled national institutions systematically and replaced them with Oromo elites and beneficiaries. This state capture changed the distribution of power, income and wealth, security arrangements, identity, land, and accountability. By all measurements on the ground concerning human life and wellbeing, Abiy Ahmed Ali is a murderer/genocider. Bloodletting of civilians he considers unworthy of life does not bother him. He undermines peace and democracy deliberately and systematically. Abiy Ahmed Ali suffers from a distorted mindset of grievance redress by punishing his enemies and opponents, slaughtering, starving, displacing, harassing, jailing primarily Amhara and Tigrayans (Abyssinians or northerners) by any means necessary. The costs are enormous. Accountability matters Abiy Ahmed Ali and partners must be held accountable for war crimes, crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing. Ethiopia will never enjoy peace without accountability. The institutional and structural changes taking place under the watch of Abiy Ahmed Ali are dramatic and irreversible. Think of the replacement of Ethiopia with Oromia; think of the change in the redesignation of Addis Ababa as Finfinnee. Think of Afan Oromo replacing Amharic as Ethiopia’s official language. There is nothing the international community would do if these were to occur. The 2018 rapprochement with Eritrea was a genuine diplomatic achievement. Yet the 2020–22 Tigray war, continuing violence in Oromia and the conflict in Amhara since 2023 reveal how fragile a settlement becomes when adversaries do not trust institutions or believe they can protect their interests peacefully. Root causes remain intact. The 2022 Pretoria agreement stopped a major phase of warfare but did not settle all underlying disputes or include all directly affected constituencies. [1–5] A viable peace process must therefore do more than obtain another ceasefire. It needs enforceable civilian-protection commitments, inclusive negotiation, independent monitoring, credible justice, space for peaceful political competition, and a negotiated approach to contested constitutional and territorial questions. No community should have to accept collective punishment, and no armed actor including the ruling party should be exempt from scrutiny. The single most critical hurdle to lasting peace and stability in Ethiopia is the Abiy ruling party and state. It is intolerant of peace and stability. It thrives on division. conflict and war. It breeds animosity and fear among ethnic and faith groups. It compromises Ethiopia’s sovereign interests by submitting itself to the UAE and its regional national goals. How does one explain Abiy Ahmed’s strategic partnership with Sudan’ s RSF? With the UAE? Why peace is illusive in Ethiopia. From the promise of 2018 to recurrent conflict Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in April 2018 and initiated reforms, including political prisoner releases and an opening of civic space. The Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 recognized particularly his role in the rapprochement with Eritrea, not a finding that Ethiopia had achieved lasting internal peace. The Nobel committee itself acknowledged the difficulty of democratization and continuing internal conflicts. [1] The question posed to the Nobel Committee is why a peace prize without demonstrated commitment to permanent peace and democratization? The transition unfolded amid longstanding grievances over centralized authority, ethnically organized federalism, political exclusion, competing territorial claims and unequal perceptions of security. Conflict between the federal government and the TPLF escalated into war in November 2020. The war involved federal, Tigrayan, Eritrean and regional forces, and devastated communities across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. The African Union-mediated Pretoria cessation-of-hostilities agreement of November 2022 reduced the fighting but left disputes over territory, displacement, implementation, and accountability unresolved. [2, 3, 6] The AU failed to demand inclusion of critical stakeholders: Afar and Amhara. In Amhara, tensions over the Pretoria process, territorial claims, and the April 2023 plan to dismantle regional special forces contributed to a confrontation between federal forces and Fano formations. In Oromia, armed conflict involving the Oromo Liberation Army and government forces persisted, accompanied by allegations of serious abuses against civilians. These conflicts have different histories; treating them as one undifferentiated rebellion obscures what each settlement must address. [2, 4, 7] Left with a sense of impunity, the Abiy government continued its assaults on civilians in the Afar. Amhara, Gambella, Oromia, Somali and Tigray regions. The latest flare between Oromo and Somali regional forces with the complicity of federal forces forced tens of thousands to flee to Kenya. In effect, Abiy Ahmed’s war is no longer confined to the Amhara and Tigray regions . It is national and regional. What the evidence shows about the democratic deficit. Freedom House’s 2026 assessment classifies Ethiopia as “Not Free,” scoring it eighteen out of one hundred, and identifies restrictions on political competition, media, civil society, due process, and independent institutions. Its Freedom on the Net report identifies connectivity restrictions in conflict-affected areas, including Amhara. These are assessments by an independent monitoring organization, not a legal determination that every government action is unlawful. [4, 8] Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026 describes continued armed conflict, serious abuses by warring parties, and restrictions on civic space. The UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia documented serious violations and abuses by multiple parties during the northern war, including war crimes and crimes against humanity. Responsibility for incidents must still be assessed on evidence, with individual accountability rather than collective blame. [2, 5] 3 | Why peace has remained elusive: Competing claims of political legitimacy Many political constituencies disagree not only about who should govern but about the rules of the state itself: the balance of federal and regional authority, the rights of individuals and communities, the electoral system, and the status of disputed territories. Without trusted procedures for resolving those questions, every major policy dispute can become a security crisis. In huge part, the reason is because Abiy Ahmed Ali has Oromoized the state and government. Non-Oromo are subject to alienation, marginalization, and submission. The option left is to defend their sheer survival. Security dilemmas and coercive disarmament When communities fear that, surrendering arms leaves them vulnerable, disarmament without credible guarantees can intensify insecurity. Conversely, the proliferation of armed forces undermines civilian authority and exposes communities to abuse. Sequenced, independently verified security arrangements are essential; neither unconditional coercion nor indefinite militarization offers a stable solution. Incomplete peace agreements and excluded stakeholders Pretoria demonstrated that negotiation could stop large-scale fighting. It also illustrates the limits of a deal that does not settle implementation, return of displaced people, disputed boundaries, and the security concerns of other affected actors. Durable arrangements must incorporate local communities, women, displaced persons, and civil society—not only the signatories who command fighters. [3, 6] Pretoria is flawed because it is not inclusive. Impunity, civilian harm, and collapsing trust Allegations of unlawful killings, arbitrary detention, attacks on health care, abductions and abuses by both state and non-state actors deepen grievances and discourage reconciliation. Independent investigations, survivor-centered remedies, and fair trials are necessary to break cycles of retaliation. The absence of trusted justice also makes ceasefires difficult to sustain. [2, 5] Humanitarian distress and regional spillover Displacement, damaged health and education systems, insecurity along transport routes, and constraints on relief access compound the political crisis. Relations with Eritrea and Sudan and disputes across the Horn of Africa add external incentives and risks. A November 2026 U.S. A Congressional Research Service report warns that overlapping rebellions and regional tensions could fuel a wider confrontation; such risk analysis should not be confused with a prediction that war is inevitable. [3, 9] The United Arab Emirates is a major component of the Ethiopian crisis. The international community must sanction this state actor that supplies drones and other weapons to Abiy’s army that in turn uses these weapons to slaughter civilians like chickens. The UAE is a destabilizing force in Africa. Independent domestic and international observers question “ Why Ethiopian elites fail to work together, do the needful and propose viable solutions with a timeframe” is baffling. What Ethiopians together can do: a practical peace architecture. First 90 days: protect lives and create a credible opening. Announce and independently monitor reciprocal civilian-protection commitments: no attacks on civilians, schools, clinics, aid workers, or civilian infrastructure; publish incident-reporting channels and rapid investigation procedures. Negotiate localized humanitarian pauses and safe access routes, with UN, Red Cross and trusted Ethiopian relief organizations assessing needs impartially across Amhara, Oromia, Tigray, Afar and other affected areas. Begin confidential exploratory talks involving federal authorities and relevant armed and civilian representatives; establish mutually acceptable mediators and guarantees against retaliation for peaceful participation. Release people arbitrarily detained, protect journalists and civil society monitors, restore communications where restricted, and enable independent observation subject to lawful security safeguards. Three to twelve months: negotiate and verify. Create an inclusive national peace forum with meaningful participation by women, youth, religious leaders, professional associations, displaced communities, minority groups, and diaspora voices; participation must not be equated with endorsing any armed group. Agree on phased ceasefires and security arrangements, with transparent benchmarks for troop repositioning, demobilization, reintegration, local policing, and protection of vulnerable populations. Establish independent, survivor-centered mechanisms for documentation, truth-seeking, reparations and prosecution of serious crimes, with safeguards for witness security and due process. Launch technical commissions on contested territories, federal-regional powers, land rights, and electoral rules; defer final decisions to legitimate constitutional and democratic procedures rather than military victory. One to three years: institutionalize peace. Strengthen electoral administration, judicial independence, parliamentary oversight and protections for opposition parties, media, and civil society. Rebuild public services and livelihoods using transparent needs-based allocations, audited funds, and community oversight; prioritize displaced people’s voluntary, safe and dignified return, or other durable solutions. Develop shared civic education and cross-community dialogue that recognize the suffering of Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, Afar, Somali, and other Ethiopian civilians without competitive victimhood. Secure regional non-interference commitments and international support for verification and reconstruction, while keeping Ethiopian communities central to decisions. 5 | Who must contribute—and what they can commit to. Federal institutions: uphold constitutional and humanitarian obligations, enable independent monitoring, negotiate in good faith, and accept impartial accountability. Armed groups: halt attacks on civilians, permit humanitarian access, reject forced recruitment, and participate in verifiable security talks. Political parties and regional administrations: pursue claims through nonviolent, transparent processes. Religious and community leaders: provide trusted spaces for dialogue without silencing victims. Diaspora organizations: support documented advocacy, relief, and bridge-building rather than dehumanizing rhetorical hold vigils and protests and highlight the tragedy inflicted on ordinary citizens by their own government that is supposed to protect them. In this connection, the protests consisting of members of the Horn of Africa in Washington on November 16 as well as those in Minnesota that issued a strong statement calling on the international community to hold the government of Ethiopia accountable are remarkable and encouraging developments. International partners: support mediation, needs-based aid, and independent accountability without imposing a political outcome. How to measure whether a peace process is real Public monthly indicators should include civilian deaths and injuries independently documented; safe humanitarian access and assistance delivered; school and clinic functionality; verified ceasefire violations; numbers of displaced people accessing voluntary durable solutions; arbitrary detention cases reviewed; participation of women and displaced communities in talks; and implementation of agreed security and justice milestones. A peace announcement without measurable improvement in civilian safety is insufficient. Conclusions Abiy Ahmed’s OPDO dominance and reconfiguration of the Ethiopian State notwithstanding, Ethiopia’s crisis cannot be explained solely by one leader, one ethnicity or one-armed movement. It is the entire system that must be overhauled. Decisions by political and military leaders’ matter, but the deeper challenge is the absence of trusted, enforceable rules for resolving disagreement. The 2018 opening showed that change is possible; the wars that followed show that ethnic elite dominated diplomacy without inclusive institutions is fragile. Assessing and critiquing the OPDO-dominated Prosperity Party is important but not enough. Ethiopia cannot afford to suffer from a mental model of permanent war. It is not a win-win model at all. It is a choice Aby Ahmed has chosen, but not for the benefit and wellbeing of the Ethiopian people. Equally, the Amhara Fano National Movement has an obligation to assess its institutional and leadership strengths and weaknesses and renew itself. The leadership must also evaluate the value added of the newly formed Alliance for Survival. Whose agenda is this new entity advancing? Long-term Ethiopians can build a more durable peace by insisting on good and democratic governance that guarantees equal civilian protection, accountable government, nonviolent political competition, genuine representation, and practical agreements whose implementation can be verified. There is no evidence that the Abiy regime is ready and willing to democratize Ethiopia. The choice of constitutional arrangements and political leadership belongs to Ethiopians through peaceful, rights-respecting processes. This is the reason a Pan-Ethiopian platform to discuss the elephant in the room–why no peace and democracy? – is essential. Finally, this author believes Ethiopians together must push for an all-inclusive series of conferences at the earliest opportunity. Initially celebrated for reforms and a peace prize for rapprochement with Eritrea, Abiy's administration has systematically dismantled national institutions, favoring Oromo elites and exacerbating ethnic tensions. The resultant violence, particularly against Amhara and Tigrayan communities, has led to accusations of war crimes and ethnic cleansing. Ethiopian News November 20, 2026 Updated: November 20, 2026 Ten Killed in Attack on Gold Mining Site and Special Forces Patrol in Bero Woreda November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Nine regional special forces members and a security guard were killed during an armed assault in Ethiopia’s Southwest Ethiopia Peoples’ Region. By Staff Writer (Nairobi, Kenya) — Armed attackers killed nine regional special forces personnel and a gold mining company security guard in Bero woreda, Southwest Ethiopia Peoples’ Region, on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, according to residents, eyewitnesses, and Deutsche Welle (DW). Eyewitnesses told DW that armed assailants targeted a gold mining site in the Chilema Shet area of Garo kebele on Wednesday morning, November 18, 2026. The attackers killed a security guard and burned company staff quarters alongside vehicles, including bulldozers and graders. One eyewitness who fled the scene stated that attackers killed special forces members attempting to defend the site. Eyewitness accounts reported by DW indicate that regional special forces traveled toward Chilema Shet from Jeba town, the administrative seat of Bero woreda, after the attack began. Assailants ambushed their patrol vehicle on the road. Nine of the ten special forces members on board died, while one survived with injuries. A relative of one victim told DW that families received the bodies of the slain personnel for burial on Wednesday and Thursday, November 19, 2026. DW reported that Bero woreda Chief Administrator Gemeda Kayidadi declined to comment. Peace and security officials in the West Omo Zone and the Southwest Ethiopia Region did not respond to phone calls seeking comment. West Omo Zone—a predominantly pastoralist area bordering South Sudan—has experienced recurring insecurity, with past attacks claiming the lives of foreign visitors, local residents, and security personnel. In a warning issued on Thursday, November 19, 2026, the U.S. Embassy urged Americans to reconsider travel to Ethiopia. The embassy advised against travel to the Tigray, Amhara, and Afar regions—specifically highlighting southern Afar and rural border areas of Tigray—and called on U.S. citizens in those areas to leave while safe to do so. BBC Amharic reported that the alert follows assessments from international outlets, including AFP and Reuters on November 18, 2026, indicating that Ethiopia and Eritrea stand on the brink of war as forces position themselves at close range along the border. Citing the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) and sources linked to armed groups, Reuters reported direct military exchanges in recent days. AFP cited analysts and foreign security sources pointing to heavy weapons attacks, cross-border incursions, and military preparations on the Ethiopian side. ACLED reported that Eritrean troops redeployed to the Badme area last week after pulling back in mid-October, massing soldiers and heavy equipment in Gwal Gemhalo and Simbel. Meanwhile, Ethiopian forces deployed close to the front line and fired heavy artillery toward positions near Badme, a contested flashpoint of the 1998–2000 war. Accounts of the fighting remain disputed. A source close to a pro-government militia in Tigray rejected reports of direct clashes with Eritrean forces. Eritrea’s Minister of Information, Yemane Gebremeskel, dismissed reports of border tensions as Ethiopian ruling-party propaganda without addressing troop deployments or fighting directly. Residents in Tigray’s North West Zone—including in Shiraro, Adi Hageray, and Biyara—told BBC Amharic that fighting involving artillery and drones pushed into rural areas earlier in the month, displacing border residents. Local officials, medical sources, and BBC Amharic accounts also reported that a drone strike in Biyara kebele near Badme on Monday, November 16, 2026, wounded at least four civilians riding in a white Isuzu pickup truck. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated sharply following Ethiopia’s push for sea access, mutual accusations involving armed groups, and severed diplomatic ties. Surging fuel costs have directly raised agricultural input expenses, notably driving up fertilizer prices. This inflation lowers crop yields and reduces purchasing power for both rural and urban households. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has ordered military action against the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), labeling them as "rogue" rulers following an attack on a military camp in Mekele, the regional capital of Tigray. The TPLF, which has distanced itself from the ruling party, had previously obstructed military movements in and out of the region. This escalation comes after a federal general was sent back to Addis Ababa upon arriving in Mekele, highlighting tensions following the TPLF's defiance of federal authority in August elections. In response to the TPLF's actions, Ahmed has called on the Ethiopian populace to support the military's operations against the TPLF, which reportedly has already begun attacking TPLF bases in Mekele. The situation underscores the ongoing conflict and instability in Ethiopia, particularly in the Tigray region, which has faced significant unrest and military confrontations in recent years.

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa 20 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has invited African leaders, health experts, and global partners to Addis Ababa for the Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), calling for collective action to build a healthier and more resilient continent. In a video message shared on social media, the Prime Minister announced that Ethiopia will host the conference from November 23 to 27 at the Addis International Convention Center. The event will be co-hosted by Ethiopia and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The conference is expected to bring together heads of state, ministers, researchers, innovators, and development partners to strengthen continental cooperation and advance African-led solutions to public health challenges, he said. PM Abiy said Ethiopia was proud to host the important gathering and looking forward to welcoming leaders, researchers, and partners from across Africa and beyond. The conference provides an important opportunity to unite knowledge, strengthen partnerships, and advance African-led solutions to the continent's health priorities, the Prime Minister underscored. "Together, let us turn shared aspirations into collective action and build a healthier, more resilient Africa," the Prime Minister underscored, adding, "Africa is ready." Held under the theme "Africa's Health Security and Sovereignty," CPHIA 2026 will focus on reducing external dependence in the health sector, strengthening resilient healthcare systems, and advancing African ownership of public health priorities. ethiopia.title: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination 20 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion By Negasi Awetehey Addis Abeba — Tigray's dynamic relationship with the modern Ethiopian state has been shaped by a historical paradox and contradiction: Tigray has been both a target of state oppression, betrayal, and genocide and, at critical moments, an influential participant in shaping the Ethiopian state itself. The Meles Zenawi era brought a long-awaited sense of relief and ecstasy to the people of Tigray after years of struggle, suffering, and uncertainty. This shift from prolonged agony to renewed hope was captured in the title of the late Dr. Solomon Enkuay's book, The Agony and Ecstasy of Tigray --a title that evokes historical contradictions: the enduring pain of oppression and conflict, alongside the exhilaration of hard-won political transformation and a new social contract. Under the EPRDF-led Ethiopian state, the people of Tigray were encouraged to believe in a shared identity founded on self-determination, equality, and mutual respect. Placing uncritical faith in the Ethiopian state, Tigrayans prioritized peace, development, and coexistence, often at the expense of safeguarding Tigray's long-term benefits. Today, that trust has been shattered, leaving behind a profound sense of collective betrayal. The promise of equality, mutual respect, and unity in diversity has become an illusion. Hated throughout history, yet ever-present Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The land of Tigray has witnessed some of the most frequent and brutal battles in human history. Millennial before the formation of Ethiopia, Tigray endured wars. Before the 2020 war, I used to hear elders saying more than 30 battles had been fought in Tigray. Figures from the center to dehumanize, especially driven by the hate of the 1970s/80s TPLF movement in the north but Tigrayans, manipulate and label it ' ሰሜኑ ሁሌ ጦርነት: የተረገመ ምድር' (the north is always at war: the cursed land). From an archaeological perspective, the earliest destruction dates back to the D'mt period (5th century BC). This was destruction of monumental temples and palaces an era when there was no world order, security and sovereignty, when a powerful empire from afar could invade any group or polity at will. Tigray, even in the age of world order and sovereignty, has endured foreign invasions and wars. Ethiopia's political sovereignty has done little to ensure the security and sovereignty of the Tigray people. Leaving ancient conflicts aside, modern wars in Tigray have put the state acting as either an indifferent or an aggressor or in alliance with the foreign forces. There was also a process that, under the guise of nation-building, the Ethiopian state fractured Tigray's territory and stripped its autonomy and capacity--deliberately leaving it weak and vulnerable to foreign invasion and internal suppression. Because the agency is in the hands of the Ethiopian state, and the same agency adding other foreign agencies has been used to invade Tigray. The 2020-2022 war waged against Tigray by the Prosperity Party-led Ethiopia demonstrates that one hardly needs to study history to witness this ugliest repetition. This government's attempt to decimate Tigray brought Eritrean forces and other drone powers with geopolitical interests. History repeats itself, but each repetition grows uglier. Another unsettling pattern for Tigray is that the broader Ethiopian populace within the country's map is not aware of Ethiopia's sovereignty and the dignity of its people. Instead, they have been manipulated into aligning with foreign forces to annihilate their own fraternal neighbor, Tigray. Meresa Tsehaye, a scholar of political science and security studies, underscores Tigray's dual position as a historically marginalized periphery within the modern Ethiopian state and a strategic part of the wider Horn of Africa. Caught between regional rivalries and competing geopolitical interests, Tigray remains vulnerable to the ambitions of global powers, Middle Eastern actors, and East African states. These overlapping geopolitical, geo-cultural, and geostrategic dynamics risk perpetuating Tigray's role as a hotspot of regional instability, where external interests overshadow its people's rights, security, and aspirations. The recurring cycle of invasion underscores the imperative of a sovereign future for Tigray. The only way to prevent war--the ugliest reality Tigrayans have abhorred throughout history, yet one that remains ever-present--is to secure the future and sovereignty. The Ethiopian government's war on Tigray started in 2020 but has never stopped. The exercise of Tigray's right to self-determination has been pushed aside. Unless this trajectory is reversed, Tigray faces the risk of being erased from the map and its people being wiped out. If this is not possible, political subjugation and assimilation remain the likely scenarios. Reversing this course is imperative for Tigray to safeguard its people, restore their dignity, and secure their right to determine their own future. Existential incompatibility of PP Ideology, Tigray nationalism The relationship between the PP's ideology and Tigrayan identity is fundamentally defined by a profound asymmetry: that between the perpetrator and the victim of betrayal, genocide, and violence. Their relationship is characterized by a fundamental contradiction--one resembling that between the killer and the killed, the perpetrator and the victim, or the betrayer and the betrayed. Although the word "Prosperity" ostensibly evokes progress, growth, and development, it has acquired an altogether different and deeply pejorative meaning in the popular consciousness of Tigray. Through a bitter linguistic play on words, Prosperity (ብልጽግና) has been recast as ብዕልግና (Biligina) in Tigrigna--a term associated with vulgarity, moral corruption, and misconduct. Consequently, Tigrayans who chose to align themselves with or join the PP came to be branded ባዕሊጉ (Baeligu), a charged label that, in this context, conveys profound condemnation of what is perceived as a betrayal of collective values, dignity, and solidarity. The post-Pretoria chapter was supposed to prove if the Prosperity Party had anything to offer Tigray--peace, justice, restoration, or rehabilitation. Instead, Tigray stood amidst ruin: over 600,000 killed, millions displaced , and its essential health, education, and transport infrastructure systematically looted and destroyed. Rather than repairing this damage , the regime has launched a new campaign to finish what it started and conquer the region completely. Ultimately, the ruling party has put nothing on Tigray's table except death or subjugation. The choice before Tigray is not simply between competing political arrangements ..." Across all phases of the war, Tigray's heritage--ancient and modern, sacred and secular--was targeted in a deliberate attempt to break a nation's spirit. From medieval monasteries to modern museums and historic icons, the assault aimed directly at what Tigrayans hold as their living soul. This physical destruction works hand-in-hand with historical abuse: through epistemic erasure, historiographical hegemony, and revisionist appropriation, ruling party figures seek to rewrite the legacy that their ethnic base belongs to the ancient legacy and history in Tigray. It is a dual-pronged strategy of cultural erasure and historical theft--destroying a people's living identity while co-opting their ancient legacy to legitimize the incumbent's party authority. Ultimately, the Prosperity Party's strategy is designed to weaken and depopulate substantive political entities like Tigray, replacing legitimate regional leadership with subservient proxies to entrench OPDO (currently, Oromo Prosperity Party) political and economic dominance. By attempting to project power into strategic maritime corridors like Assab, the ruling apparatus seeks to consolidate indefinite and irreversible rule--a centralized trajectory that is fundamentally incompatible with Tigray's historical identity and current struggle for self-determination. Self-Determination: Earned, learned, and craved Let us consider the words of Ms. Atsede Gebremedhin (a member of Tigray's 'Shig Weyane' (Revolutionary Torch) in the 1980s. She emphasized her message in Tigrigna, essentially conveying that although her generation envisioned Tigray's future within a federal framework, Ethiopian unity must never be traded for subjugation. When the choice is between self-determination and slavery, the pursuit of independence becomes unavoidable. Her words underscore a timeless principle: no political arrangement is worth sacrificing a people's freedom, dignity, and right to determine their own future. She further detailed her position, which can be, excerpted from the full speech, distilled into the following terms: "...regarding separation [from Ethiopia], we choose separation [independence]. Father Kidanu has been saying, 'We have separation as a second option.' We are putting it as an option, but if a progressive government is promulgated in Ethiopia, it [separation] will not be put as an option. It should not be taken that way. Only if a reactionary and slave system is to come to Ethiopia, we will have to separate ourselves to escape the slavery [oppression]. Therefore, separation is from the slavery and not from working-class people of Ethiopia." More than four decades later, Tigray has endured not only prolonged instability but also the devastating crime of genocide. Its longstanding adversaries, having regrouped after their defeat, returned with renewed force to inflict another wave of devastation marked by persecution, torture, genocide, and betrayal. These experiences have brought the question of self-determination back to the forefront of political consciousness. The aspiration for independence has increasingly gained prominence, finding expression through diverse political platforms, organized movements, public discourse, and cultural expression. Music, in particular, has become an important vehicle for expressing Tigrayan identity, historical consciousness, and national aspirations. Songs such as ዓዲ ኣላትኒ (I Have a Country), ሃ ገር እየ ዝደሊ (What I Want Is Independence), ትግራዋነት (The Essence of Being Tigrayan), ትግራይ ዓደይ (Tigray, My Nation), ትግራይ ኵሕሎ (Beautiful Tigray), ት ግራይ ምልባማ (Tigray, the Land of Wisdom), and many others reflect the growing significance of national identity, belonging, and aspirations for a sovereign future. This aspiration is neither new nor detached from history. It is rooted in generations of struggle and shaped by the historical experience of imperial nation-building and its devastating consequences for Tigray. It has been earned through sacrifice, strengthened by historical experience, and sustained by an enduring desire for freedom and a secured future. Yet, alongside this growing sense of national purpose, one fundamental question remains: How can this aspiration be translated into a viable, sustainable, and peaceful political future for Tigray? One step into a cruel destiny For the Prosperity government, war has served--and continues to serve--as an instrument for breaking the will, resistance, and collective determination of the people of Tigray. When the regime deploys starvation, foreign military forces, political coercion, and the co-optation of local elites to subdue an entire population, the struggle for self-determination ceases to be merely a political preference. It becomes an indispensable safeguard against subjugation and the permanent erosion of a people's freedom. A sober assessment of post-Pretoria reveals a deeply unsettling reality: Tigray appears to be entering the opening phase of a cruel political destiny--subjugation under the rule of the Prosperity government. As Tigray remains unliberated and increasingly subjected to the authority of the central regime, Ethiopia's overriding objective appears to be the dismantling of the political and institutional foundations that sustain Tigray's resistance and struggle for self-determination. Under the guise of pacification and political normalization, the federal government, helped by some Tigrayans who made their peace with the prime minister, appears to be pursuing a strategy of neutralizing resistance through the co-optation of Tigray's political and military elites. By offering administrative appointments, financial and material inducements, and assurances of personal survival, it seeks to hollow out the liberation struggle from within. Former defenders of Tigray's political aspirations risk becoming instruments and mouthpieces of the very central authority they once opposed. This political realignment risks a deeper ideological capitulation. A collective consciousness once anchored in freedom, dignity, and self-determination is gradually giving way to enforced subjugation and political assimilation. As former defenders align themselves with the very authority they once opposed, the moral and political foundations of the struggle erode, undermining its unifying force and leaving society increasingly disarmed--both politically and psychologically--and pressured to surrender long-term freedom for the precarious promise of immediate stability and survival. For those aligned with Abiy Ahmed's government, life under external control appears increasingly acceptable and normal. For those who continue to resist, however, subjugation remains unacceptable at any cost. Meanwhile, the central regime and its local partners increasingly portray the historical struggle led by the TPLF as outdated, destructive, or an obstacle to "peace and development." As these narratives take hold, submission risks being recast as political pragmatism, while historical memory and collective political consciousness are distorted or erased. Future generations may consequently be led to view the sacrifices of their predecessors and the TPLF's struggle not as acts of resistance and defense of the right to self-rule but as misguided and costly mistakes. Coercive assimilation, state-led social engineering What is presented as integration may, under occupation and political subordination, become a state-engineered project of assimilation. By extending central government institutions and security structures into Tigray's social and political life, the state could displace local authority, dismantle sovereign institutions, and erode the foundations of self-governance. Prolonged military occupation could thus serve not merely to administer territory but to impose a far-reaching political and social transformation. This process could entail the imposition of political, cultural, and administrative arrangements through military coercion, legislative control, divide-and-rule tactics, and the systematic suppression of local autonomy. Rather than recognize Tigray's distinct historical experience and political aspirations, the central state could seek to remake its institutions and public life in its own image and in accordance with its political priorities. The danger extends beyond institutional control to demographic and territorial engineering. In the aftermath of mass atrocities, such developments raise grave concerns about whether political domination could evolve into a broader project of demographic transformation, threatening the long-term continuity of the Tigray people. As this trajectory becomes entrenched, many Tigrayans--particularly those unwilling to abandon the pursuit of self-determination--may come to see leaving their homeland as the only remaining means of resisting subjugation. Those who remain, meanwhile, could find themselves trapped in a deeply fractured society, divided between accommodation and resistance, privilege and deprivation, and outward compliance and inward resentment. Tigray risks becoming a society of happy slaves and unhappy slaves--one in which subjugation is normalized for some and silently endured by others. This division between those aligned with the central government and those resisting subjugation could harden into an entrenched system of divide and rule. By cultivating competing loyalties and interests within Tigrayan society, the regime could fracture collective solidarity, weaken organized resistance, and obstruct a unified political response. The result could be an "enemy within" syndrome, in which internal suspicion becomes a major obstacle to future unity. Mutual distrust could gradually replace the quiet solidarity, shared understanding, and knowing glances through which Tigrayans sustained one another during the darkest years of siege and blockade. A society once united by shared suffering and resistance could become consumed by suspicion over who has accommodated the system, who has resisted it, and who can still be trusted. Indefinite social discord The existing horizontal divisions within Tigrayan elites--expressed through political realignments, competing strategic visions, and conflicting interpretations of the postwar order--risk hardening into a prolonged and intergenerational rupture. If centralizing and assimilationist policies become entrenched, Tigray could face not only a political struggle over its future but also an internal war over its history, identity, and collective memory. Self-determination must once again become the organizing principle of Tigray's political future." One generation may grow increasingly exposed to central government-sponsored narratives, while another remains committed to preserving Tigray's historical struggle for self-rule rights, convictions, and aspirations. Such a rupture would not remain confined to political organizations or public institutions. It could penetrate the most intimate structures of the society. The long-term damage would extend far beyond political disagreement, undermining the social trust upon which collective life depends. The collapse of social contract of sacrifice Perhaps one of the most devastating long-term consequences of an unaddressed political defeat and perceived internal betrayal would be the destruction of society's capacity for collective mobilization. When the social contract of sacrifice is broken, a profound cynicism may take hold toward political leadership, military institutions, and the very causes for which ordinary people were once prepared to make extraordinary sacrifices. For a population to endure the horrors of war, there must be a fundamental, often unspoken covenant among the people, their fighters, their leadership, and the cause they serve. That covenant rests on a shared understanding: sacrifice must have meaning; those who fall must be remembered and honored; the suffering of the population must not be exploited; and leaders must not trade away the collective cause for their personal security or political survival. When this covenant is violated, the consequences can endure for generations. The public may lose confidence in those who call for sacrifice, and future appeals for mobilization may be met with profound skepticism. People may no longer regard military mobilization as an honorable defense of their homeland and collective aspirations but as a political instrument through which ordinary citizens bear the ultimate costs while political and military elites negotiate their own survival and interests. The memory of betrayal can therefore become a powerful deterrent to future collective action. Even when an existential threat emerges, a population that has lost confidence in its leadership may hesitate to mobilize, fearing that its sacrifices will once again be squandered or betrayed. The f
ethiopia.summary: Tigray's complex relationship with Ethiopia is marked by historical oppression and betrayal, juxtaposed with moments of significant political influence. The era of Meles Zenawi initially brought hope to Tigrayans, who believed in a shared identity based on self-determination and equality. However, this trust has been shattered, revealing a deep sense of betrayal as the Ethiopian state has failed to protect Tigray's autonomy and rights. The 2020-2022 war exemplified this betrayal, leading to immense loss of life and destruction of infrastructure. The Prosperity Party's ideology has further marginalized Tigray, fostering resentment and a desire for self-determination among its people. Cultural erasure and historical appropriation have compounded these grievances, as Tigrayans seek to reclaim their identity and future. ethiopia.content: Eritrea: U.S. Lawmaker Proposes Trade Incentives to Push Ethiopia, Eritrea Off Conflict Cliff, Toward Peace - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Eritrea: U.S. Lawmaker Proposes Trade Incentives to Push Ethiopia, Eritrea Off Conflict Cliff, Toward Peace Ayin Network TPLF fighters (file photo). 20 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — US Republican Representative Jim Baird has proposed two pieces of legislation seeking to link expanded trade and economic cooperation with Ethiopia and Eritrea to progress toward lasting peace, as tensions between the neighboring countries continue to raise fears of a renewed interstate conflict. The proposed Ethiopia SPARK Act and Eritrea PILLAR Act would use US agricultural exports, farm equipment, technical expertise and cooperation in critical minerals development as economic incentives for both countries to pursue peace, according to a report by The Hill published on November 19. The legislation, shared exclusively in draft form with The Hill , also seeks to strengthen US economic influence in the Horn of Africa and reduce China's foothold in the region. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Under the proposed measures, Ethiopia and Eritrea would be offered opportunities for formal trade negotiations and expanded access to US agricultural products, including corn, soybeans, soybean meal and livestock feed, as well as farm machinery, agricultural research and technical assistance, contingent on steps toward establishing lasting peace. The proposals also envisage US assistance in developing the region's mineral resources, including gold, silver, copper, zinc, iron ore, potash, cement, limestone, natural gas and oil, alongside cooperation on port infrastructure. Washington could offer reduced tariffs and improved trade terms as additional incentives. Baird, a Republican from Indiana and member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Africa, described the initiative as an opportunity to build economic partnerships with African countries while limiting the influence of US adversaries. "African nations are primed for partnership," Baird said in a statement to The Hill . "The continent is rich in natural resources and home to a young, growing population eager for greater economic opportunity. In Indiana and across America's heartland, we have the agricultural expertise and technological know-how to help unlock that potential and build lasting economic partnerships." "East Africa has tremendous potential, with the benefit of limited influence from America's adversaries, like China," he added. Baird said the proposed economic cooperation could provide a foundation for regional stability and prosperity, arguing that African countries pursuing peaceful cooperation and economic growth would find a willing partner in the United States. The initiative comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with competing claims over sovereign Red Sea access, mutual accusations of interference and reported military buildups along their shared border heightening fears of a wider confrontation. The deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries broke down on October 1, following Ethiopia's closure of its embassy in Asmara and the expulsion of Eritrean diplomats, a move reciprocated by Eritrea . Both governments have subsequently exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, while reports of troop movements, drone strikes and artillery activity around the disputed border town of Badme have intensified concerns about a possible military escalation.
